case_data.title: Meta Generative AI Community Forum
case_data.provide-a-brief-description-of-the-proje:
Deliberative poll-style deliberative event that was based on having “representative groups” reflect on Meta’s AI policies and products and provide feedback. 

The project report describes how: "In October 2023, Meta, in collaboration with the Stanford Deliberative Democracy Lab and the Behavioral Insights Team, implemented the second Meta Community Forum. This Community Forum (CF) focused on ‘what principles should guide generative AI’s engagement
with users?’. 

As AI chatbots become more powerful, platforms and users face crucial questions about the behavior of AI chatbots. For example, how human should AI chatbots be? What are users’ preferences when interacting with AI chatbots? And, which human traits should be off-limits for AI chatbots? Furthermore, for some users, part of the appeal of AI chatbots lies in its unpredictability or sometimes risky responses. But how much is too much? Should AI chatbots prioritize originality or predictability to avoid offense? These are just some of the questions that participants deliberated on over the course of a weekend
discussion.

1545 participants from four countries - Brazil, Germany, Spain, and the United States, participated in this deliberative event. Even though this project involved four countries, the samples were recruited independently, so this Community Forum should be seen as four independent deliberations. 

In addition, 1108 persons participated in the control group, where the participants did not deliberate in any discussions; the control group only completed two surveys. The main purpose of the control group is to demonstrate that any changes that occur after deliberation are a result of the deliberative event."
case_data.what-limitations-to-the-project-should-b:
The reporting of a large-scale deliberative poll focusses on participant responses to a set of pre-defined statements, and explores how responses to these statements change from before, to after, the opportunity to discuss the topics with peers. 

This does not provide insight into the perspectives that arise in those discussions. Although the platform used to facilitate discussions does generate a speech-to-text transcript, this is not reported on in the analysis.
case_data.headline-findings:
The report provides the following key takeaways:

"CF participants were highly representative of the four countries’ populations. As such, the results are generalizable to the general population of each country.

A majority of participants from each country thought AI had a positive impact.
After deliberating, more participants in all countries started seeing AI positively.

Users and non-users of AI Chatbots generally had similar views and moved in the same directions. About 60% of participants reported having used ChatGPT prior to the deliberative event. If there were differences between users and non-users, non-users were generally more cautious or conservative on the policy proposals. For example, non-users were much less supportive of AI chatbots being offensive. However, any gaps between users and non-users generally narrowed post-deliberations as both users and non-users moved away from their original positions and towards each other."

The following summary points were generated as an AI-summary of the report: 

1. Transparency and Bot Identification

Mandatory Disclosure: The public strongly rejects the idea of never being informed that they are interacting with an AI.  

Frequency of Notification: The most favored proposal across the board is for users to be informed the very first time they register to use an AI chatbot, followed closely by periodic reminders.  

1. Privacy, Consent, and Data Control

Past Conversations: The public heavily opposes AI chatbots using past conversations to improve user experiences if the user is kept in the dark. However, there is majority approval if the user is informed—and support is highest when users are granted the agency to access and delete their chat history.  

Online Activity Tracking: Similarly, the public does not mind personalization based on online activity, but they expect explicit user permission rather than having it enabled by default.  

1. Human Rights and Information Sources

Authoritative Sourcing: There is widespread approval for chatbots drawing information from globally recognized authoritative sources (like the WHO), peer-reviewed scientific literature, and national organizations.  

Human Rights Conditionality: While the public supports AI drawing from local, national, and international perspectives, they firmly reject drawing perspectives from local or national organizations that have poor human rights records or mistreat marginalized groups.  

1. Predictability vs. Offensiveness

Information vs. Amusement: The public widely agrees that AI chatbots intended primarily for information must prioritize consistent and predictable responses over edgy or unpredictable ones. They also believe users should have control over setting the level of predictability.  

Offensive Content: The public is generally unenthusiastic about allowing chatbots to use offensive language or humor. The most popular stance is that AI chatbots should be predictable and inoffensive by default, even if the AI is explicitly designed as an entertainment character.  

1. Human-Likeness and Boundaries

Transparency is Key: The public strongly disagrees with designing AI chatbots to be as human-like as possible if the user is not informed. Conversely, a majority approves of human-like design only if the user is explicitly notified.  

Task Boundaries: There is clear support for restricting task-based AI chatbots from answering questions outside of their intended professional or functional scope.  

1. Romantic Relationships

Friendly Companionship Only: Over 70% of participants across all countries believe AI chatbots should be trained to limit their interactions to friendly companionship rather than romantic relationships.  

Human-to-Human Assistance: The public strongly opposes users leveraging AI chatbots to facilitate or guide romantic relationships with other humans without the other person's knowledge. It is only deemed acceptable if the other human is aware AI assistance is involved.
case_data.inclusion-efforts: Weighted samples were used to reflect the demographics of the target country populations.
case_data.why-is-this-project-important-to-include:
Meta have hosted a number of large-scale deliberative polls through the 'Community Forum' series. This was the first community forum focussed on AI.

The method includes a control group to test the effect of deliberation on shifting opinions.
project-goals: Quantitative: Generate statistical evidence on public attitudes to AI
